claim: Recent research suggests that brain-heart interactions are associated with perceptual and self-consciousness.
source: Recent research suggests that brain-heart interactions are associated with perceptual and self-consciousness.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by references to prior research in the field.

claim: Neural responses to visceral inputs have been hypothesized to play a leading role in shaping our subjective experience.
source: In this line, the neural responses to visceral inputs have been hypothesized to play a leading role in shaping our subjective experience.
evidence: This is a hypothesis statement based on theoretical developments in the field.

claim: The local-global paradigm evaluates the capacity of a patient to detect the appearance of auditory irregularities at local (short-term) and global (long-term) levels.
source: EEG recordings were taken during the local-global paradigm, which evaluates the capacity of a patient to detect the appearance of auditory irregularities at local (short-term) and global (long-term) levels.
evidence: This describes the experimental paradigm used in the study.

claim: Local and global effects produce distinct ERPs and HERs that can help distinguish between minimally conscious state and unresponsive wakefulness syndrome patients.
source: The results show that local and global effects produce distinct ERPs and HERs, which can help distinguish between the minimally conscious state and unresponsive wakefulness syndrome patients.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on experimental data.

claim: ERP and HER responses were not correlated, suggesting that independent neuronal mechanisms are behind them.
source: Furthermore, we found that ERP and HER responses were not correlated suggesting that independent neuronal mechanisms are behind them.
evidence: This is a finding from correlation analysis in the study.

claim: HER modulations in response to auditory irregularities, especially local irregularities, may be used as a novel neural marker of consciousness.
source: These findings suggest that HER modulations in response to auditory irregularities, especially local irregularities, may be used as a novel neural marker of consciousness and may aid in the bedside diagnosis of disorders of consciousness with a more cost-effective option than neuroimaging methods.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: Theoretical developments in consciousness and experimental research have rooted the basis of consciousness in how the brain responds to visceral inputs.
source: Theoretical developments in consciousness and experimental research have rooted the basis of consciousness in how the brain responds to visceral inputs (Azzalini et al., 2019; Candia-Rivera, 2022a; Park and Tallon-Baudry, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: In post-comatose patients, the consciousness diagnosis is primarily based on behavioral signs of consciousness.
source: In post-comatose patients, the consciousness diagnosis is primarily based on behavioral signs of consciousness (Bayne et al., 2017), which aims at distinguishing between patients showing only reflex-like responses to the environment, diagnosed as Vegetative State or Unresponsive Wakefulness Syndrome (VS/UWS; Laureys et al., 2010), and patients with fluctuating but reproducible signs of non-reflex behavior, diagnosed as a Minimally Conscious State (MCS), (Giacino et al., 2002), but see also Naccache, 2018.
evidence: This describes standard clinical practice supported by citations.

claim: Behavioral assessment is not sufficient and neuroimaging techniques are used to detect covert states of consciousness.
source: However, recent results demonstrate that behavioral assessment is not sufficient and neuroimaging techniques are used to detect covert states of consciousness (Kondziella et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to recent research.

claim: The classification of MCS and UWS patients using EEG and cardiac features while undergoing processing of auditory regularities has shown an advantage over EEG features alone.
source: The classification of MCS and UWS patients using EEG and cardiac features while undergoing processing of auditory regularities has shown an advantage over EEG features alone (Raimondo et al., 2017), implying that brain-heart interactions may be involved in the conscious processing of auditory inputs.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: Brain-heart interactions may be involved in the conscious processing of auditory inputs.
source: The classification of MCS and UWS patients using EEG and cardiac features while undergoing processing of auditory regularities has shown an advantage over EEG features alone (Raimondo et al., 2017), implying that brain-heart interactions may be involved in the conscious processing of auditory inputs.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited study.

claim: Automatic classifications of HERs in the resting-state showed that these markers may capture residual signs of consciousness.
source: Recent evidence on automatic classifications of HERs in the resting-state showed that these markers may capture residual signs of consciousness (Candia-Rivera et al., 2021a; Candia-Rivera and Machado, 2023a) suggesting that HERs might convey state-of-consciousness relevant information about how the brain responds to bodily-related stimuli.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: HERs might convey state-of-consciousness relevant information about how the brain responds to bodily-related stimuli.
source: Recent evidence on automatic classifications of HERs in the resting-state showed that these markers may capture residual signs of consciousness (Candia-Rivera et al., 2021a; Candia-Rivera and Machado, 2023a) suggesting that HERs might convey state-of-consciousness relevant information about how the brain responds to bodily-related stimuli.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from cited research.

claim: In healthy participants, the processing of auditory stimuli may cause cognitive modulations to the cardiac cycle.
source: Further evidence exists in healthy participants, in which the processing of auditory stimuli may cause cognitive modulations to the cardiac cycle (Tanaka et al., 2023; Marshall et al., 2022; Banellis and Cruse, 2020; Perez et al., 2020; Pfeiffer and De Lucia, 2017), and HERs correlate with perceptual awareness (Al et al., 2020; Banellis and Cruse, 2020; Park et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: HERs correlate with perceptual awareness.
source: Further evidence exists in healthy participants, in which the processing of auditory stimuli may cause cognitive modulations to the cardiac cycle (Tanaka et al., 2023; Marshall et al., 2022; Banellis and Cruse, 2020; Perez et al., 2020; Pfeiffer and De Lucia, 2017), and HERs correlate with perceptual awareness (Al et al., 2020; Banellis and Cruse, 2020; Park et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: HERs can be modulated by contextual processing of different levels of auditory regularities, as presented in the local-global paradigm.
source: We hypothesized that HERs can be modulated by contextual processing of different levels of auditory regularities, as presented in the local-global paradigm (Bekinschtein et al., 2009).
evidence: This is the main hypothesis of the study.

claim: The study analyzed HERs following the presentation of auditory irregularities, with special regard for distinguishing UWS (n=40) and MCS (n=46) patients.
source: In this study, we analyze HERs following the presentation of auditory irregularities, with special regard for distinguishing UWS (n=40) and MCS (n=46) patients.
evidence: This describes the study design and sample size.

claim: The automated classification of this cohort was previously performed in another study.
source: Note that the automated classification of this cohort was previously performed in another study (Raimondo et al., 2017).
evidence: This references a prior study on the same cohort.

claim: The study employed high-density EEG recordings to assess the cognitive processing of auditory irregularities in patients with disorders of consciousness using the local-global paradigm.
source: This study employed high-density EEG recordings to assess the cognitive processing of auditory irregularities in patients with disorders of consciousness using the local-global paradigm (Bekinschtein et al., 2009).
evidence: This describes the methodology of the study.

source: In XX blocks, frequent stimuli consisted of five equal sounds (local and global standard), whereas infrequent stimuli had four equal sounds followed by a different 5th sound (local and global deviant).
evidence: This describes the experimental design as shown in Figure 1A.

claim: In XY blocks, frequent stimuli involved four equal sounds followed by a different 5th sound (local deviant and global standard), while infrequent stimuli featured five equal sounds (local standard and global deviant).
source: In XY blocks, frequent stimuli involved four equal sounds followed by a different 5th sound (local deviant and global standard), while infrequent stimuli featured five equal sounds (local standard and global deviant).
evidence: This describes the experimental design as shown in Figure 1A.

evidence: This is a statistical result from cluster permutation analysis shown in Figure 3A.

evidence: This is a statistical result from cluster permutation analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The HER local effect was larger than what would be expected by chance as estimated from surrogate heartbeats (Monte Carlo p=0.03).
source: The HER local effect was larger than what would be expected by chance as estimated from surrogate heartbeats (HER local effect, Monte Carlo p=0.03; HER global effect, Monte Carlo p=0.54).
evidence: This is a statistical result from surrogate analysis.

claim: The HER global effect was not significantly larger than what would be expected by chance as estimated from surrogate heartbeats (Monte Carlo p=0.54).
source: The HER local effect was larger than what would be expected by chance as estimated from surrogate heartbeats (HER local effect, Monte Carlo p=0.03; HER global effect, Monte Carlo p=0.54).

claim: A significant ERP and HER local effect was found in both MCS and UWS patients.
source: We found a significant ERP and HER local effect in both MCS and UWS patients.
evidence: This is a finding from statistical tests shown in Table 1.

claim: The global effect was significant only for MCS patients in both ERP and HER analysis.
source: On the other hand, the global effect was significant only for MCS patients in both ERP and HER analysis.
evidence: This is a finding from statistical tests shown in Table 1.

claim: This result extends previous reports highlighting the predictive power for the conscious state of the global effect.
source: This result extends previous reports highlighting the predictive power for the conscious state of the global effect (Pérez et al., 2021).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results in the context of prior research.

claim: The measured effects do not show apparent correlations between ERPs and HERs for local and global effects.
source: In Figure 4A are presented all pair comparisons between ERPs and HERs. for local and global effects. The figure depicts that the measured effects do not show apparent correlations (details on Spearman correlation tests in Table 2).
evidence: This is a finding from correlation analysis shown in Figure 4A and Table 2.

claim: The four markers (ERP global, ERP local, HER global, and HER local) present complementary information for the separation of the diagnostic groups.
source: Figure 4B shows that the four markers: ERP global, ERP local, HER global, and HER local present complementary information for the separation of the diagnostic groups.
evidence: This is an observation from the visualization in Figure 4B.

claim: Combining HER local, ERP global, and ERP local offered the most complementary information out of all possible triads, achieving a cross-validation accuracy of 79.1%.
source: Figure 4C illustrates that combining HER local, ERP global, and ERP local offered the most complementary information out of all possible triads, achieving a cross-validation accuracy of 79.1%.
evidence: This is a result from the classification analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The accuracy improved to 80.2% when incorporating all four features.
source: The accuracy further improved to 80.2% when incorporating the four features.
evidence: This is a result from the classification analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: HERs provide additional insights in conjunction with the standard ERP analysis.
source: These findings highlight the additional insights provided by HERs in conjunction with the standard ERP analysis.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the classification results.

claim: HER average during the whole protocol presents a small, clustered effect when comparing MCS and UWS patients.
source: HER average during the whole protocol presents a small, clustered effect when comparing MCS and UWS patients (Figure 5A, left).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: A higher HER variance is observed in MCS compared to UWS during the whole protocol.
source: In Figure 5A, the right panel is shown that a higher HER variance is observed in MCS compared to UWS during the whole protocol.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: A wide scalp coverage presents higher HER variance in MCS, as compared to UWS (cluster permutation test, p<0.0001, Z=4.0772, latency = 20–500 ms).
source: A wide scalp coverage presents higher HER variance in MCS, as compared to UWS (cluster permutation test, p<0.0001, Z=4.0772, latency = 20–500 ms).
evidence: This is a statistical result from cluster permutation analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Brain-heart interactions have demonstrated to be involved in consciousness and relevant for the clinical assessment of brain-injured patients.
source: Considering that brain-heart interactions have demonstrated to be involved in consciousness and relevant for the clinical assessment of brain-injured patients (Candia-Rivera et al., 2021a; Candia-Rivera and Machado, 2023b; Perez et al., 2020; Raimondo et al., 2017; Riganello et al., 2019), we analyzed neural responses to heartbeats during the processing of auditory irregularities to characterize MCS and UWS patients.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The processing of short- and long-term auditory irregularities shows distinctive responses between MCS and UWS patients in their HERs.
source: The processing of short- and long-term auditory irregularities, i.e., the local and global effects, shows distinctive responses between MCS and UWS patients in their HERs.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings of the study.

claim: The EEG signals synchronized to heartbeats (HERs) provided complementary information to the ERPs synchronized to auditory irregularities.
source: The correlation analyses revealed that the EEG signals synchronized to heartbeats (HERs) provided complementary information to the ERPs synchronized to auditory irregularities.
evidence: This is a finding from the correlation analysis.

claim: Examining the local effects using HERs and ERPs yielded better differentiability between MCS and UWS patients.
source: Examining the local effects using HERs and ERPs yielded better differentiability between MCS and UWS patients (see Figure 5).
evidence: This is an observation from the analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: The HER local effect demonstrated higher specificity, as only 3% of randomly timed surrogate heartbeats exhibited separability that surpassed what was observed with the original heartbeats.
source: It is worth noting that the HER local effect demonstrated higher specificity, as compared to the HER global effect during the permutation test. Only 3% of randomly timed surrogate heartbeats exhibited separability that surpassed what was observed with the original heartbeats.
evidence: This is a finding from the surrogate analysis.

claim: These results align with previous findings that suggest the existence of a short-term auditory-cardiac synchrony.
source: These results align with previous findings that suggest the existence of a short-term auditory-cardiac synchrony (Banellis and Cruse, 2020; Pérez et al., 2021; Pfeiffer and De Lucia, 2017).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results in the context of prior research.

claim: Brain-heart dynamics may serve as markers of the conscious processing of auditory information, particularly in distinguishing short-term changes.
source: Moreover, our findings indicate that brain-heart dynamics may serve as markers of the conscious processing of auditory information, particularly in distinguishing short-term changes.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the study's findings.

claim: Automatic classifications of these patients showed a higher accuracy when locking EEG to heartbeats, with respect to the classification of EEG segments unrelated to the cardiac cycle.
source: Our results go in the same direction as previous evidence, in which automatic classifications of these patients showed a higher accuracy when locking EEG to heartbeats, with respect to the classification of EEG segments unrelated to the cardiac cycle (Candia-Rivera et al., 2021a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The measured responses in ERPs and HERs do not separate MCS and UWS patients' groups completely.
source: Nevertheless, the measured responses in ERPs and HERs do not separate MCS and UWS patients' groups completely (see Figure 4C), suggesting that some patients do not react or only react to some trials that were attenuated when averaging all trials in the time-locked analysis.
evidence: This is an observation from the classification results shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The ERP global effect observed in healthy controls did not follow the same trend as MCS patients.
source: Furthermore, it is worth noting that the ERP global effect observed in healthy controls did not follow the same trend as MCS patients.
evidence: This is an observation from the data analysis.

claim: The response observed in healthy controls resembles a standard P300 response.
source: However, the response observed in healthy controls does resemble a standard P300 response.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on knowledge of ERP components.

claim: The ERPs during local deviants exhibit superior discriminatory ability between MCS and UWS patients.
source: These findings align with previous reports indicating that the ERPs during local deviants exhibit superior discriminatory ability between MCS and UWS patients (Faugeras et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Both ERP and HER in processing local auditory irregularities might be predominant for distinguishing between MCS and UWS.
source: Furthermore, these results suggest that both ERP and HER in processing local auditory irregularities might be predominant for distinguishing between MCS and UWS.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the study's findings.

claim: The inclusion of global effects marginally improved the classification performance.
source: Nonetheless, the inclusion of global effects marginally improved the classification performance, indicating that although the global effects are weaker than the local effects, they might provide complementary information to the local effects.
evidence: This is a finding from the classification analysis.

claim: Brain-heart interactions, as measured with HERs, are related to perceptual awareness.
source: Our results contribute to the extensive experimental evidence showing that brain-heart interactions, as measured with HERs, are related to perceptual awareness (Azzalini et al., 2019; Skora et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Neural responses to heartbeats correlate with perception in a visual detection task.
source: For instance, neural responses to heartbeats correlate with perception in a visual detection task (Park et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: A higher detection of somatosensory stimuli occurs when the cardiac cycle is in diastole and it is reflected in HERs.
source: Further evidence exists on somatosensory perception, where a higher detection of somatosensory stimuli occurs when the cardiac cycle is in diastole and it is reflected in HERs (Al et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Heart transplanted patients show that the ability of heartbeats sensation is reduced after surgery and recovered after one year, with the evolution of the heartbeats sensation recovery reflected in the neural responses to heartbeats.
source: Evidence on heart transplanted patients show that the ability of heartbeats sensation is reduced after surgery and recovered after one year, with the evolution of the heartbeats sensation recovery reflected in the neural responses to heartbeats as well (Salamone et al., 2020).

claim: The responses to heartbeats covary with self-perception: bodily-self-identification of the full body.

claim: Brain-heart interactions measured from heart rate variability correlate with conscious auditory perception.

claim: The neuronal mechanisms behind ERPs and HERs responses are independent.
source: These results suggest that the neuronal mechanisms behind these ERPs and HERs responses are independent.

claim: HER variance is higher in MCS patients than in UWS patients, as previously reported in resting state.
source: In addition, we found that HER variance is higher in MCS patients than in UWS patients, as previously reported in resting state (Candia-Rivera and Machado, 2023a).

claim: There are two distinct neuronal signatures that set apart patients in a MCS from those in an UWS.

source: Such ERPs and HERs modulations by conscious access to a new stimulus attribute may well correspond to a self-consciousness updating process occurring 'downstream' to conscious access (Sergent and Naccache, 2012), and enabled, for instance, in a global neuronal workspace architecture (Dehaene and Naccache, 2001).
